entries.title: link installed Nish packages' agent skills into .claude/skills
entries.body:
`npm install nish` in a project now links the writing-nish skill into `.claude/skills/`, where coding agents load project skills from. The new `npx nish-skills` command links the skills of every installed Nish package (one whose exports use the `nish` condition) after a library is added. A package ships a skill as `skills/<name>/SKILL.md`. The links are relative symlinks into `node_modules/` (junctions on Windows), so they follow upgrades, and nish claims its own skill names before any library can.

Nish only touches its own links, the ones pointing inside the project's `node_modules/`. A skill directory or link you made is never replaced or removed, and a `.claude` that is itself a link is left unwritten. Links to packages you uninstall are pruned. Nothing is linked for a global install, under npx, or with `NISH_NO_SKILLS` set, and a failed link never fails the install. In a workspace, both postinstall and `nish-skills` link at the root nish is installed in. The new Agent skills guide page says what is linked, how to opt out, and how a library ships its own skills.
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: Http1Connection says when it is between requests
entries.body:
`Http1Connection.betweenRequests()` answers whether a graceful drain may close the connection without cutting a request short. It is true in the HTTP state with no request open, no head begun to arrive, and nothing waiting to be written.

Since 0.36.0 `requestOpen` is private. A program that drained its own server had to combine that field, the head clock and `wantsWrite()` to answer this question, and it can no longer read the first. The connection now answers the question itself, so those fields stay private. The http-server guide shows the drain loop. A program that feeds a connection itself calls `headArrived` after each feed, as the built-in carriers do, so a head that has begun to arrive counts.

entries.title: pin vector 0.2.1 and run the spec tests in CI
entries.body:
nish now pins @amritk/vector 0.2.1 in .vector-version. scripts/fetch-vector.sh clones that tag and builds build/vector/dist/vector; npm still serves only 0.1.0, so the pin is a git tag. Vector 0.2.1 reads spec sources only as RFC text or kramdown-rfc XML, and it refused the old Markdown hex spec. So specs/hex.md is now kramdown-rfc, built to specs/hex.xml with scripts/build-spec.sh (copied from vector, MIT). contracts/hex.json is extracted from that XML and test/spec/hex.ts is 0.2.1's emit of it. Their requirement, exclusion, function and clause ids are unchanged.

tests/run.js gains a `spec` section, run in CI's first shard. For each generated test it requires the contract and a single vector-contract-sha256 line equal to the contract's hash. When the target module exists in std/, it builds and runs the test. A stale or failing test is a FAIL; a module not landed yet (nish/hex today) is a named SKIP.

rfcs/ holds RFC 4231, 4648, 5869, 7748, 8032 and 8439 unmodified, with their kramdown-rfc references in .refcache/ and their notices in THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md. scripts/check-filenames.mjs exempts .refcache/, whose names kramdown-rfc fixes.

Vector 0.2.1 cannot set a property's sample count from a spec. The hex properties therefore run vector's default of 26 to 39 samples where the hand-written contract asked for 96; contracts/README.md records this.

entries.title: hold nish/crypto/chacha20poly1305 to RFC 8439 with a vector contract
entries.body:
std/crypto/chacha20poly1305.ts is now held to RFC 8439 by a vector 0.2.1 contract that takes the RFC as its main source. Every requirement is quoted from the RFC, and every MUST in it is tested or excluded with its reason. The test vectors come from sections 2.3.2, 2.4.2, 2.5.2, 2.6.2, 2.8.2 and A.5, and 13 properties sit beside them. All 15 requirements pass, and CI runs the generated test through the `spec` section.

The spec is vector's own at v0.2.1, copied under its MIT notice and listed in THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md. chacha20QuarterRound (whose u32[] state vector's types cannot express) and chacha20HeaderMask (RFC 9001) are recorded as untested in the spec, because vector 0.2.1 cannot declare outOfScope exports from a spec.

entries.title: hold nish/crypto/hkdf to RFC 5869 with a vector contract
entries.body:
std/crypto/hkdf.ts is now held to RFC 5869 by a vector 0.2.1 contract that takes the RFC as its main source. Every requirement is quoted from the RFC. hkdfExtractSha256 and hkdfExpandSha256 are checked against the PRK and OKM of Appendix A's test cases 1 to 3, and five properties check them against hmacSha256. All 8 requirements pass, and CI runs the generated test through the `spec` section.

The spec is vector's own at v0.2.1, copied under its MIT notice and listed in THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md. The other exports of nish/crypto/hkdf are recorded as untested in the spec, each with its reason, because vector 0.2.1 cannot declare outOfScope exports from a spec: SHA-384, the Secret, Expand-Label (RFC 8446), Into and Held variants, and HkdfScratch.

entries.title: hold nish/crypto/hmac to RFC 4231 with a vector contract
entries.body:
std/crypto/hmac.ts is now held to RFC 4231 by a vector 0.2.1 contract that takes the RFC as its main source. Every requirement is quoted from RFC 4231's section 1 definitions and section 4 test cases. hmacSha256, hmacSha384 and hmacSha512 are checked against the 18 known answers of test cases 1 to 4, 6 and 7. Properties check the HMAC construction over sha256, sha384 and sha512, the long-key path and the tag length, and CI runs the generated test through the `spec` section.

Test case 5 prints only a 128-bit truncation, and a vector row must hold a function's whole return value, so its three answers are properties. The verify functions are recorded as untested, with the other exports of nish/crypto/hmac, because RFC 4231 does not specify them; tests/link/crypto_hmac covers them in nish.

entries.title: hold nish/crypto/ed25519 to RFC 8032 with a vector contract
entries.body:
std/crypto/ed25519.ts is now held to RFC 8032's PureEdDSA Ed25519 by a vector 0.2.1 contract that takes the RFC as its main source. Every requirement is quoted from sections 5.1, 5.1.5, 5.1.6 and 5.1.7. The public keys of all five section 7.1 tests are vector rows. Properties check signing and verification: the public-key and signature sizes, sign-then-verify, refusal of a flipped signature or message bit, S out of range, and truncated inputs. CI runs the generated test through the `spec` section.

vector 0.2.1 refuses the section 7.1 signature rows. A Call label cannot hold the RFC's "MESSAGE (length 1 byte)", a plain "MESSAGE" label fails fidelity, and TEST 1's empty message is printed only as a length. Its exact refusals are recorded, and tests/link/crypto_ed25519/rfc.ts still checks those five signatures. Ed25519ctx, Ed25519ph and Ed448 are outside the profile: nish implements PureEdDSA Ed25519 only.
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: hold nish/crypto/x25519 to RFC 7748 with a vector contract
entries.body:
std/crypto/x25519.ts is now held to RFC 7748 by a vector 0.2.1 contract that takes the RFC as its main source. Every requirement is quoted from sections 5, 5.2 and 6.1, and every MUST is tested or excluded with its reason. x25519 and x25519Base, whose scalars are secret-bytes, are checked against section 5.2's two single-step vectors and its 1-iteration vector. Properties cover input and output sizes, top-bit masking, non-canonical inputs, clamping, the base point, and both sides of section 6.1's Diffie-Hellman exchange, whose printed keys and shared secret they assert. CI runs the generated test through the `spec` section.

Two vector 0.2.1 limits shape the contract. Fidelity needs a row's label to be the RFC's printed name, such as "Alice's private key, a", and a label cannot spell the apostrophe, comma or parentheses, so section 6.1 stays a property its bytes are not checked against. The 1,000-iteration vector cannot be chained without printed intermediates. The 1,000,000-iteration vector is excluded for its run time, X448 is outside the profile, and the f25519 internals are recorded as untested.

entries.title: stop the docs landing hero playing twice on a first load

entries.title: WP63 S2 — io_uring slot handles in nish:net
entries.body:
A `nish:net` listener opened with `NET_LISTEN_RING` (flag 8) on Linux accepts into io_uring ring slots instead of descriptors. Slot handles are `i32`s at 2^20 and above. `netRead`, `netWrite`, `netClose`, `pollAdd`, `pollRemove` and `pollWait` take them as they take descriptors. One listener serves 3,000 loopback connections under a descriptor limit of 1,024, with fewer than 64 entries in `/proc/self/fd`. Where the kernel refuses rings (seccomp, `io_uring_disabled`, an old kernel), the listener serves descriptors, and the new `netRingState()` reports why: 1 for rings, 0 for none yet, a negative errno for a refusal. The bit is opt-in.

A slot's unsent bytes are bounded at 256 KiB, past which `netWrite` answers -11. A full set answers -23 from `tcpAccept`. A slot's receive is held once 256 KiB is queued, so a peer the program does not read stalls in the kernel. A close with sends queued lingers until they are sent. `pollWait` keeps a share of each batch for descriptors when ring slots fill it, so `signalFd()` is still reported. Once a ring listener exists, a signal reaches a loop through `signalFd()` rather than by ending `pollWait` early. A set that fails to open, and a transient failure of the first one, fall back to descriptors without latching. A reset slot fails writes with its errno and is never re-armed. An accept that finds the kernel short of memory (-12, -105) answers that errno once, then pauses accepting for 10 ms, doubling to 640 ms while the shortage lasts, and accepts again.

The security record is docs/security/net-uring.md, NURING-1 to NURING-29. The guide's networking page and docs/LANGUAGE.md describe the surface. The text budgets of runtime-net.c and runtime-uring.c grow to 11,008 and 7,424 bytes.

entries.title: link a package's agent skills only when the user accepts them
entries.body:
Installing nish no longer links any agent skill into a project. A skill is instructions for a coding agent plus, optionally, tools it may use without asking: `allowed-tools`, `hooks`, or a shell command run when the skill loads. Linking every installed Nish package's skills at install time let any dependency hand the project's agent that power unasked, and a link silently followed every later upgrade. Postinstall now writes nothing and prints one line pointing at `npx nish-skills`.

`npx nish-skills` lists each skill a Nish package ships, with its package and version, description and every grant, and links only the ones you accept:
- On a terminal it asks y/N for each one, and the default is no.
- Without a terminal it links the skills you name, or every grant-free skill with `--yes`.
- A skill that grants anything is linked only when you name it.

An acceptance is recorded in `.claude/skills/.nish-skills.json` against the package, the skill and a hash of the skill's whole directory. A changed skill, or another package's skill under the same name, is unlinked until you accept it again.

The frontmatter reader fails closed. Anything it cannot read as plain `key: value` lines, any key outside a fixed list of inert ones, any load-time shell syntax, and any link, special file or unreadable entry in the skill all count as grants. No display limit can hide a grant from the question. The trust model is on the agent-skills guide page, and SC-35 in docs/security/supply-chain.md records the finding.

entries.title: add --debug-arena, which traps a stale arena reference
entries.body:
`nish compile --debug-arena --link` and `nish run --debug-arena` link a runtime whose arena never reuses an address. A reference kept past the scope that allocated it faults on its first use and the runtime names it as a stale arena reference, rather than reading whatever the arena wrote there next. The emitted IR is the same either way, and a normal link is unchanged.

Every arena chunk is exact, one block per chunk, so each allocation and rewind goes through the runtime. Chunks are page-aligned spans of one PROT_NONE reservation, and a release turns them PROT_NONE again (falling back to a 0xDB fill). A SIGSEGV/SIGBUS handler on the alternate stack reports the fault and re-raises it. The flag is native-only: it is refused without a link, and under the wasi and wasm profiles.

All 935 `tests/cases` programs with an expected output were linked against the debug runtime, and none held a stale reference.

entries.title: give the docs site a share card, page metadata and a clearer header
entries.body:
Links to nishlang.com unfold into a share card made from the hero (docs/site/og.png, rendered by scripts/gen-og-image.mjs). The new docs/site/page.js writes schema.org structured data on every page and rewrites it on client-side route changes. nishlang.com is now the project's homepage. The header leads with Get started, then GitHub and the Language reference. Module names in tables break only after a slash, and each word of the hero's name eases open to its own width.

The soundness run's ASan builds now link every runtime unit, runtime-uring.c among them. Without it, every generated program failed to link and the nish-cmp elision rows ran out of time. The golden cases' Nish runner gets 20 minutes instead of 15, since a slow runner passed every case and was then cancelled.

entries.title: NL9018 warns when a handler the loop calls drops a temporary
entries.body:
NL9018 now counts what a pass keeps at any depth of calls. A function the loop calls is charged to the loop when it answers no memory, has no scope of its own, and builds and drops a temporary on every call that returns, or calls a function that does. A branch on a parameter against a constant still counts as every call, which is how a handler dispatches on its event. The warning names the call and the site, and its rewrite puts the arena block in the function that builds the temporary. --emit-arena marks that site "accumulates": true.

The sweep this enabled fixed two real leaks: CapabilityLock.readVersion kept a substring per key, and FetchSyncClient.drain built a 4 KiB buffer per redirect hop.
metrics: VmRSS after 2,000 then 20,000 requests on one keep-alive connection, 5 runs each, growth identical to the kB across runs: helper_leaky +1,252 kB and method_leaky +1,252 kB, both unwarned before; each arena rewrite +0 kB

entries.title: move to vector 0.3.1, restore hex's 96 samples, print the staleness check
entries.body:

A test now passes only if at least one of its clauses passed: a test whose every clause was skipped, such as one made only of slow iterated vectors, fails with "no clause passed", as vector's own run calls it an error. Each clause a test skips is reported as a SKIP. CI emits tests without --slow, so slow iterated vectors run by hand with `vector spec run --slow`. contracts/README.md and .claude/orientation.md describe the pin and the 0.3.x spec features (samples, outOfScope, Iterate).

entries.title: WP63 S3 — restricted io_uring rings under --sandbox
entries.body:
A --sandbox program granted `net` but not `process.spawn` keeps the ring bit. Before the seccomp filter loads, the runtime makes the rings its ring listeners will use. Each ring is created with IORING_SETUP_R_DISABLED and given IORING_REGISTER_RESTRICTIONS:
- SQE_OP allows ACCEPT, RECV, SEND, CLOSE, ASYNC_CANCEL and NOP only.
- SQE_FLAGS allows FIXED_FILE, BUFFER_SELECT and CQE_SKIP_SUCCESS only.
- No register op is allowed.
Its file table and buffer ring are registered, and then it is enabled.

The filter then kills io_uring_setup and io_uring_register. It allows io_uring_enter only on a premade ring's descriptor, and kills all three when no ring was made. A sandboxed program cannot make a ring, lift a ring's restrictions, or drive a ring that it inherited or that was moved onto another descriptor number. Without `net` all three stay killed. With `net` and `process.spawn` nothing changes.

How many rings, and whether to make any, is decided at build time. The ring count is the root package.json's `"nish": { "netRings": N }`, from 1 to 64 with a default of 1; a value out of range is NL3058. The compiler records whether `main` can reach NET_LISTEN_RING. It counts any flags argument it cannot prove leaves bit 8 clear, and makes no ring when the bit is unreachable.

docs/security/sandbox.md gives the three-way rule, the new step and its checks. docs/security/net-uring.md records:
- NURING-33 to NURING-37, including NURING-36, which stays open: a foreign ring moved onto a premade ring's number can still be entered;
- the io_uring CVEs since 5.10, each with whether a restricted ring reaches it, with the unclassified ones listed.
The sandbox guide page explains `netRings` and how to size it. The WP63 roadmap marks S3 done, and D2 is decided.
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: WP63 S4 — HandlerLimits listen on io_uring rings, and the entry re-measured
entries.body:
`nish/net/handler` can hold connections past the descriptor limit. `HandlerLimits` gains `ring`, and `listen(host, port, backlog, flags)` sets NET_LISTEN_RING on the listener when `ring` is on. `slots` is the connection cap, and it is no longer bounded by RLIMIT_NOFILE. A listener whose rings are all full answers -23 from tcpAccept. The handler rests on that the way it rests on -24, and a close ends the rest early. The new `HttpHandler.resting()` reports whether it is resting. A kernel that refuses rings serves descriptors, and `netRingState()` says why. The defaults are unchanged: 256 slots and no ring.

`bench/http1-server.ts` and the new `bench/handler-ring/` take BENCH_RING=1. The entry, with SQLite on every request, was measured as one ring process against five epoll processes, in 5 interleaved rounds against a byte-identical epoll copy:
- At 18,000 connections, a request costs 25.63 µs against 34.60, 25.9% less.
- At the box's C of 96,000, it costs 26.20 against 37.17, 29.5% less.
The verdict against the design note's §4 is go. The ring process holds about four times the memory a connection at 96,000 (2.8× at 18,000), so D1 stays opt-in. The WP63 roadmap marks S4 done, and the design note records the measurement and D1.

This also corrects the nish-cmp DECLARED changelog words for #1679's entry to match that PR's merged subject.
metrics: 25.9% at 18k and 29.5% at 96k against 0.5% and 0.7% median bands; per-round bands up to 3.9%, smallest per-round saving 24.1%

entries.title: std/net/oidc — OpenID Connect discovery and a rotating JWKS key set
entries.body: Adds std/net/oidc (nish/net/oidc). Given an issuer URL, it finds the provider's signing keys through OpenID Connect discovery, keeps them current as they rotate, and verifies tokens with nish/crypto/jwt. The key decides the algorithm, never the token. A cross-origin jwks_uri is fetched under an outbound policy that allows public addresses only. Security record: docs/security/oidc.md.

entries.title: keep each premade ring's number on its ring under --sandbox
entries.body:
The seccomp filter lets io_uring_enter take only the premade rings' descriptor numbers, but it cannot see the file behind a number. Code holding a ring made outside the sandbox could move it onto a premade ring's number (dup2/dup3, or close plus F_DUPFD, including a number a closed ring listener freed) and enter it (NURING-36).

nish_uring_premake now makes a keeper ring, disabled, restricted to NOP and never enterable. Under --sandbox, close, dup2 and dup3 onto a ring's or the keeper's number kill the process, except dup3 from the keeper. close_range answers ENOSYS. ur_free_ring drops a pooled ring with dup3(keeper, fd), so no ring number is ever free.

Also from #1690: a --sandbox fallback test where no ring is premade, net_handler_ring running past a descriptor limit of 32, a tls: log line in the h2 interop server, and per-CVE verdicts in the io_uring record. The unclassified CVE records are not listed by ID.

Tests: tests/link/sandbox_fixtures (324 passed; the before run fails 10)
Refs: docs/security/net-uring.md

Fixes #1690

entries.title: propose WP48 again as 32-bit references for linked classes
entries.body:
WP48 declined a whole-program 32-bit reference mode on 2026-11-11. The Goose
ports show a node with no lean layout left: tree.ts's node is 24 bytes where
Goose's is 12. This note proposes a narrower design. The compiler picks
compact classes (a native executable, a link field that saves bytes, made in a
loop or recursion, nothing forbidding it), keeps their instances 4-byte aligned
in one reserved range, and stores only a field typed as that class as an i32
offset. `implements Compact` and `implements Wide` force or refuse it, and a
program with no compact class compiles to the same IR as before.

It follows the first note's order: the arena on a reserved range first
(measured free), then the decode measured on bench/wp48-refs/sibling.ts before
any emitter work. A stage covers the compiler's and std's own classes. Nothing
in src/, runtime/ or std/ changes yet.

entries.title: measure mmap_size and a shared cache on the five-process entry
entries.body: WP63 S5 measures the design's two cheaper wins for the multi-process entry against the unchanged five epoll processes, on the S4 stand-in: PRAGMA mmap_size saves 15.7% of server CPU per request, a nish/sync/shm cache 14.9%, and a per-worker private cache shows no measurable change. bench/handler-ring/wins.sh reruns the comparison; WP63 is landed, 6 of 6.
metrics: mmap −15.7%, shm cache −14.9%, private −2.0% (medians of 7 rounds; noise band 0.6% between medians, 6.0% worst single round)

entries.title: code that decides what a package may grant fails closed
entries.body: A CLAUDE.md rule under Security, from the review of #1669. Anything that reads package-controlled input to decide whether to ask the user uses an allowlist of what is inert. It treats everything else, and anything it cannot parse, as a grant, and it never lets a length cap drop a grant from the question. The same root cause recurred in five review rounds of that PR.
